title: Implant complications & peri-implant disease
blurb: Peri-implant mucositis versus peri-implantitis, the other things that can go wrong with implants, and how good maintenance keeps an implant healthy.
question: A patient had an implant crown fitted three years ago. She says the gum around it bleeds when she brushes and she has a bad taste. She smokes and stopped coming for hygiene reviews. What could be happening around the implant, and why does it matter more than bleeding around a natural tooth?

teach.h: An implant is not a tooth
teach.body: A dental implant is a titanium (sometimes zirconia) fixture placed in the jawbone. Over several months the bone bonds directly to its surface: osseointegration. An abutment and crown are then attached. There is no periodontal ligament, so no shock absorber and less 'feel' when biting. The gum fibres run alongside the implant instead of inserting into it, so the seal is weaker and infection can track down to the bone faster. Implants can't decay, but plaque still builds up on them and causes disease.

teach.caption: Bleeding on probing happens in BOTH. Bone loss and deepening pockets are what make it peri-implantitis.

steps.label: Implant failure
steps.sub: Mobility, then loss of the implant

teach.caption: Mucositis is the stage to catch: with better cleaning and professional care, it can resolve completely.

teach.caption: Anything a patient reports about an implant, from bleeding to looseness to numbness, is passed straight to the dentist.

items: Clean around the implant crown twice a day with a soft brush, plus interdental brushes, floss or a water flosser.
Attend regular reviews: the dentist or hygienist checks bleeding, pus and pocket depths, and takes radiographs to monitor bone.
Professional cleaning uses instruments that won't scratch the implant surface, such as plastic or titanium tips.
Stop smoking and keep diabetes well controlled.
Report bleeding, a bad taste, swelling or looseness early, before bone is lost.

teach.text: Mucositis = soft tissue only, no bone loss, reversible. Peri-implantitis = bone loss, not reversible. Don't pick the answer that says peri-implantitis is 'just inflammation of the gum'.

items: Implants are held by bone directly (osseointegration): no PDL and a weaker gum seal.
Peri-implant mucositis: like gingivitis; soft tissue only; reversible.
Peri-implantitis: like periodontitis; progressive bone loss; can lead to implant failure.
Risks: plaque, history of periodontitis, smoking, diabetes, excess cement, missed reviews.
Other problems: failed integration, nerve damage, sinus perforation, loose screws, chipped crowns.

summary: You can now explain why an implant is more vulnerable than a natural tooth, tell peri-implant mucositis from peri-implantitis, list the risk factors and other complications of implant treatment, and give the maintenance advice that keeps an implant healthy.

A.q: The tissue around a patient's implant is red and bleeds on gentle probing, but radiographs show no bone loss. Which condition is this?
A.why: Inflammation of the soft tissue around an implant without bone loss is peri-implant mucositis, the implant equivalent of gingivitis.

whyNot.0: Peri-implantitis involves loss of supporting bone.
whyNot.1: Failed osseointegration means the bone never bonded to the implant, which would make it loose.
whyNot.3: Periodontitis affects natural teeth, not implants.

A.q: Which feature distinguishes peri-implantitis from peri-implant mucositis?
options: Bleeding when the area is probed
A.why: Bone loss around the implant is what defines peri-implantitis. Bleeding, redness and swelling occur in both conditions.

whyNot.0: Bleeding on probing occurs in both conditions.
whyNot.1: Redness is a sign of inflammation in both conditions.
whyNot.2: Swelling of the soft tissue occurs in both conditions.

A.q: Why can infection spread to the bone more quickly around an implant than around a natural tooth?
options: It has no ligament and a weaker seal
Implants have a nerve supply that fails
Implant crowns are always made too short
A.why: Implants have no periodontal ligament, and the gum fibres run alongside rather than inserting into the implant, so the soft-tissue seal is weaker.

whyNot.0: Plaque builds on any surface; the issue is the weaker tissue seal.
whyNot.2: Implants have no nerve supply of their own.
whyNot.3: Crown length is not the reason infection spreads faster.

B.q: Which is a recognised risk factor for peri-implantitis?
B.why: Patients who have had periodontitis are at higher risk of peri-implantitis, along with smokers, people with diabetes and those who miss maintenance.

whyNot.1: Fluoride toothpaste protects natural teeth and is not a risk factor.
whyNot.2: Fissure sealants are a caries-prevention measure and are not linked to implant disease.
whyNot.3: Water fluoridation is not linked to peri-implant disease.

B.q: A patient says his implant crown feels slightly loose and turns when he touches it, but there is no pain or bleeding. What is a likely cause?
B.why: A crown that rotates without pain or inflammation often has a loose abutment screw, a common mechanical complication. The dentist needs to see it.

whyNot.0: Mucositis causes bleeding and redness, not a loose crown.
whyNot.1: Sinus perforation is a surgical complication in the upper jaw, not a cause of a loose crown years later.
whyNot.3: Nerve damage causes numbness or tingling, not looseness.

options: No, the bone loss is permanent
Yes, with better cleaning and care
B.why: Mucositis involves soft tissue only, so improved home cleaning and professional care can resolve it.

whyNot.0: There is no bone loss in mucositis; that is peri-implantitis.
whyNot.2: Removal is not needed for mucositis.
whyNot.3: Mucositis is managed by removing plaque, not long-term antibiotics.

C.q: Which cleaning aid is most suitable for daily cleaning around an implant crown?
C.why: Interdental brushes clean the sides of the implant crown where plaque gathers, without damaging the surface or the gum.

whyNot.1: Metal instruments can scratch the implant surface and injure the gum.
whyNot.2: Hard bristles can damage the soft tissue seal.
whyNot.3: Whitening pastes are often abrasive and don't clean between the teeth.

C.q: The day after an implant was placed in the lower jaw, a patient phones to say her lower lip and chin still feel numb. What should you do?
options: Tell her it is normal for several weeks
Advise a warm salt-water mouth rinse
Book her a routine review next month
C.why: Numbness persisting after the anaesthetic should have worn off may mean damage to the inferior alveolar nerve, which the dentist must assess urgently.

whyNot.0: Prolonged numbness is not normal and must not be dismissed.
whyNot.1: Rinsing will not help nerve damage, and the dentist needs to know now.
whyNot.2: Waiting a month could delay management of a nerve injury.

C.q: Which sequence shows how implant disease usually progresses?
C.why: Plaque first inflames the soft tissue (mucositis); if untreated, bone is lost (peri-implantitis), which can end in implant failure.

whyNot.0: Mucositis comes before peri-implantitis, not after.
whyNot.2: Disease doesn't start with mucositis before health, and failure is the end point.
whyNot.3: Failure is the final stage, not the second.

reteach.title: Gingivitis and periodontitis, but around a screw
reteach.question: You already know how gum disease affects natural teeth. What happens when the same process happens around an implant?

blocks.body: Around a natural tooth, plaque first causes gingivitis: red, bleeding gums, no bone loss, fully reversible. Left alone it becomes periodontitis, with bone loss that can't be undone. Implants follow the same story: mucositis is the 'gingivitis' stage and peri-implantitis the 'periodontitis' stage. The difference is that an implant has no periodontal ligament and a weaker gum seal, so it can move to the bone-loss stage faster and is harder to treat.

blocks.h: Stage 1 on a natural tooth: gingivitis
blocks.caption: Inflamed gum, bone level normal. Around an implant, this stage is peri-implant mucositis: reversible.

blocks.h: Stage 2 on a natural tooth: periodontitis
blocks.caption: Bone lost and a pocket formed. Around an implant, this stage is peri-implantitis: not reversible.

blocks.text: Implants can't get caries, but they CAN get gum and bone disease. A patient who thinks an implant 'needs no looking after' is at risk.

explain.body: Bone bonds directly to the titanium surface (osseointegration) over several months. There is no periodontal ligament, and the gum fibres run alongside the implant rather than into it. This weaker seal is why implant disease can reach bone quickly.

steps.label: Osseointegration
steps.sub: Bone bonds to the surface over months

options: The gum attaching to a crown
Bone bonding directly to an implant
A ligament forming around an implant
test.why: Osseointegration is the direct bonding of living bone to the implant surface, which holds the implant firm.

whyNot.0: Gum attachment is part of the soft-tissue seal, not osseointegration.
whyNot.2: No periodontal ligament forms around an implant.
whyNot.3: Cement setting is about fixing the crown, not the implant in bone.

explain.body: Plaque inflames the soft tissue around the implant: redness, swelling and bleeding on probing, but no bone loss. It is reversible with better home cleaning and professional cleaning.

options: Bone loss with pus and implant mobility
A crown that turns when touched
test.why: Mucositis is inflammation confined to the soft tissue around the implant, with no bone loss.

whyNot.0: Bone loss, pus and mobility describe advanced peri-implantitis.
whyNot.2: Numbness suggests nerve damage after surgery.
whyNot.3: A rotating crown suggests a loose screw.

explain.body: Inflammation spreads to the bone, which is progressively lost. Signs include bleeding, pus, deeper pockets and bone loss on radiographs; late on the implant becomes mobile. It can be halted but not reversed, and may end in implant loss.

explain.caption: The natural-tooth equivalent: periodontitis, with bone loss and a pocket.

test.q: Which investigation shows whether bone has been lost around an implant?
test.why: Radiographs show the bone level around the implant and are compared over time to detect bone loss.

whyNot.0: Blood glucose relates to diabetes control, not bone level.
whyNot.1: Vitality tests check a natural tooth's pulp; implants have none.
whyNot.3: Caries dye is for decay, which implants cannot get.

explain.body: Daily cleaning with interdental aids, regular reviews with radiographs, stopping smoking and good diabetes control protect implants. Also recognise surgical problems (infection, nerve damage, sinus perforation) and mechanical ones (loose screws, chipped crowns), and pass any concern to the dentist.

rows.label: Bleeding or bad taste around the implant
Numb lip or chin after lower-jaw surgery

test.q: Which lifestyle advice most reduces the risk of peri-implantitis?
test.why: Smoking impairs healing and blood supply and is a major risk factor for peri-implantitis and implant failure.

whyNot.1: Milk does not affect the risk of peri-implant disease.
whyNot.2: Food temperature does not cause peri-implantitis.
whyNot.3: Chewing on one side does not prevent implant disease.
